title: The Washington Eight Win in Berlin
text:
The University of Washington crew that went to the 1936 Berlin Olympics was made up largely of the sons of loggers, farmers and fishermen, young men working their way through college in the Depression. One of them, Joe Rantz, had been left to fend for himself as a teenager when his family moved away without him.

Coach Al Ulbrickson spent seasons shuffling rowers until he found a combination that moved as one. Their boat, the Husky Clipper, was built by George Pocock, an English boatbuilder who also coached them in technique. Pocock taught that a crew wins when all eight oars catch and release in perfect rhythm, a feeling rowers call swing, and that a man has to trust the others completely to find it.

The final at Grunau on 14 August was stacked against them. They had drawn the most exposed lane, their stroke, Don Hume, was sick, and they did not hear the start, so they began well behind. Coxswain Bobby Moch kept the stroke rate low for most of the race, then called for more and more in the final stretch, with Hume barely able to see. In front of a crowd that included Hitler, they caught Italy and Germany and crossed the line first, by about six tenths of a second.

None of the nine was a famous athlete, and most had not rowed before college. Together, they won Olympic gold.
lesson: Some results come only when everyone trusts the others enough to stop pulling alone. Look for rhythm and trust in a team, not just raw strength.
people: Joe Rantz, Al Ulbrickson, George Pocock, Bobby Moch, Don Hume
source: Daniel James Brown, The Boys in the Boat (2013); official report of the 1936 Olympic Games
